To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a variable stiffness actuation can be used as a natural way to mimic a pair of antagonistically acting muscles, and that the control of such a system can be performed by mapping the muscle activations, estimated via EMG, on the exo-actuator inputs.
a variable stiffness actuation can be used for assistive applications and that the muscle-like behavior of the actuator can be exploited for control.

a variable stiffness actuation can be used to mimic the human muscle dynamics and a control policy based on the analogy between the exoskeleton and the muscle systems can be used to reduce the subject muscle effort.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the design of a novel variable stiffness actuator and with a novel control policy based on the analogy between the exoskeleton and the muscle system, to be exploited to assist the user in the execution of tasks.
the design of an assistive device that can be controlled by the subject, exploiting the subject's own control system, and that can be used in a wide variety of applications.
the design of a new type of variable stiffness actuation, and the development of a control strategy to exploit it.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the FLExo is a promising platform to assist the upper limbs of people suffering from muscle weakness, as well as a novel approach to control variable stiffness actuated devices.

FLExo is a variable stiffness assistive device, whose control parameters are analogous to human muscle parameters, and that the control policy is able to exploit this analogy in order to provide an effective and natural interaction.
the proposed approach is able to reduce the subject effort by a 50% on a simple task.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have designed, controlled and tested a new exoskeleton with variable stiffness, based on the analogy of the muscle system.
the proposed exoskeleton is capable of reproducing the behavior and the dynamics of the natural system.
the proposed device is a step forward towards a more natural control of assistive robots, by exploiting the muscle-like behavior of the mechanical device.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a muscle-like actuator, when controlled by means of a proper feedforward mapping of the estimated muscle activations, allows for a substantial reduction of effort in a wide variety of tasks, from static to dynamic ones.
the proposed control strategy is effective in terms of reduction of effort, and that the exoskeleton is capable of reproducing a muscle-like behavior.
a muscle-like variable stiffness device can be used for assistive purposes, with a simple and intuitive control policy, based on the estimation of human muscle activations.
